 3                                          I.    INTRODUCTION

 4   Q.     PLEASE STATE YOUR NAME AND BUSINESS ADDRESS

 5   A.     My name is Dave Elliott. I hold the title of Manager, Transmission Line Design

 6          Engineering at LCRA. My business address is 3505 Montopolis Drive, Austin, TX 78744.


 7   Q.     PLEASE DESCRIBE YOUR PROFESSIONAL QUALIFICATIONS.

 8   A.     I hold a bachelor’s degree in civil engineering from the University of Missouri – Columbia.

 9          I have nearly twenty years of professional experience in engineering design and

10          maintenance of overhead transmission lines. I have worked at three different electric

11          utilities, including Kansas City Power & Light (now Evergy), Ameren, and LCRA, where

12          I have been employed since 2022. I have held multiple roles within the design, operations,

13          and project execution departments at those organizations, including Transmission Line

14          Design Engineer, Supervisor of Transmission Line Maintenance Engineering, and my

15          current role, where my primary responsibility is leading engineering and design teams in

16          the execution of overhead transmission line projects. I am a registered Professional

17          Engineer in the State of Texas (License No. 159061).

18                 One of the projects I am responsible for is the proposed Bell County East Switch –

19          Big Hill Substation 765 kilovolt (kV) transmission line project (Proposed Transmission

20          Line Project or Project), for which Oncor Electric Delivery Company LLC (Oncor) and

21          LCRA Transmission Services Corporation (LCRA TSC) (together, the Applicants) seek

22          approval in this proceeding. My educational and professional qualifications are more fully

23          presented in my resume, which is attached hereto as Exhibit DME-R1.



     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                Page 3
  1                                II.   PURPOSE OF REBUTTAL TESTIMONY

 2   Q.     DID YOU FILE DIRECT TESTIMONY IN THIS DOCKET?

 3   A.     No, I did not.


 4   Q.     WHAT IS THE PURPOSE OF YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY?

 5   A.     The purpose of my rebuttal testimony is to testify on behalf of the Applicants in support of

 6          the Application to amend their certificates of convenience and necessity (CCN) in this

 7          proceeding. More specifically, I respond to certain engineering, construction, vegetation

 8          management, and maintenance concerns, recommendations, and other issues raised in

 9          intervenor testimony regarding engineering and cost portions of the Application, as well as

10          post-approval construction and maintenance activities. I have been and remain actively

11          involved in LCRA TSC’s engineering planning and development of the Proposed

12          Transmission Line Project, and I address the following: specific concerns regarding the

13          design of 765 kV transmission line facilities; questions regarding the Applicants’ specific

14          construction and maintenance practices; assumptions regarding the size, scale, and

15          appearance of the Applicants’ proposed transmission line facilities; and concerns regarding

16          electric and magnetic field (EMF) effects of 765 kV lines on existing and future

17          infrastructure. I also describe the Applicants’ coordination on the development of the

18          engineering and cost components of the Application. Finally, I respond to intervenor

19          concerns regarding the Applicants’ ability to execute a first-in-Texas 765 kV project and

20          describe the engineering due diligence that Applicants have executed to date to ensure the

21          delivery of a safe and reliable project.




     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                 Page 4
 1    Q.     WAS YOUR REBUTTAL TESTIMONY PREPARED BY YOU OR UNDER YOUR

2           DIRECT SUPERVISION AND CONTROL?

3    A.     Yes.


4            III.   OVERVIEW OF INTERVENORS’ ENGINEERING, CONSTRUCTION,
5                                AND MAINTENANCE CONCERNS

6    Q.     PLEASE       GIVE      A    BRIEF      OVERVIEW          OF      THE     ENGINEERING,

7           CONSTRUCTION,              AND    MAINTENANCE             CONCERNS          RAISED        IN

8           INTERVENOR TESTIMONY.

9    A.     Hundreds of intervenors filed direct testimony in this docket, many of which expressed

10          concerns about engineering, construction, and maintenance related matters. The specific

11          issues fall into several broad categories, including the size and appearance of the Project’s

12          facilities, health and safety concerns, compatibility with commercial operations, cost

13          estimates, existing and planned facilities both within and outside of the Project’s proposed

14          right-of-way (ROW), audible noise emanating from high-voltage power lines, and the

15          Applicants’ understanding of and familiarity with 765 kV overhead transmission lines. I

16          address the specific issues raised within each category below.




     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                  Page 5
  1             IV.    REBUTTAL REGARDING THE SIZE AND APPEARANCE OF THE
 2                                  PROJECT’S FACILITIES

 3   Q.     THE DIRECT TESTIMONY OF MULTIPLE INTERVENORS DESCRIBED THE

 4          PROJECT TO INCLUDE 300 FOOT-TALL TOWERS.                                GIBBONS RANCH

 5          LIMITED          PARTNERSHIP          (PAGE       13)    DESCRIBES          THE      TOWER

 6          FOUNDATIONS BEING “UP TO 50’ X 50’ EACH.” PLEASE CONFIRM THE

 7          HEIGHT AND DIMENSIONS OF A TYPICAL TANGENT TOWER AND ITS

 8          FOUNDATIONS.

 9   A.     The heights and dimensions described by these intervenors are inaccurate and are more

10          consistent with wind turbine structures, not the proposed 765 kV facilities. As described

11          in the Application, the height of typical structures ranges from 155-160 feet for Oncor and

12          140-170 feet for LCRA TSC. The estimated maximum height of the structures above

13          ground is 198 feet. These dimensions may vary depending on the terrain and other

14          engineering constraints, such as crossing existing transmission lines. While the overall

15          footprint of a typical tower is approximately 50 feet by 50 feet, the foundation itself consists

16          of four symmetrically placed piers ranging from four feet in diameter to eight feet in

17          diameter each.




     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                     Page 6
  1   Q.     THE DIRECT TESTIMONIES OF MULTIPLE INTERVENORS DESCRIBE THE

 2          PROJECT’S TOWER BEING OUTFITTED WITH FEDERAL AVIATION

 3          ADMINISTRATION            (FAA)    WARNING         LIGHTS.         PLEASE DESCRIBE

 4          APPLICANTS’ PROCESSES FOR EVALUATING IMPACTS TO AIRSPACE

 5          AND THE NEED FOR WARNING LIGHTS ON THIS PROJECT.

 6   A.     Applicants’ top priority is to maintain safe navigation space for aircraft. In general,

 7          however, it is not anticipated that most towers constructed for the Project will require FAA

 8          warning lights. Once the Commission selects a final route, Applicants will coordinate their

 9          proposed locations and heights of each tower with the FAA through their pre-screening

10          tool. If that tool flags a specific location, Applicants will submit their proposed structure

11          to the FAA for further study. In cases where the FAA determines that a structure poses a

12          potential hazard to navigation, Applicants will first pursue alternative design solutions

13          (e.g., structure modifications or minor reroutes) to avoid the installation of FAA warning

14          lights on a given tower. Applicants will install warning lights only if other design

15          alternatives cannot ensure safe navigation of airspace. Ms. Cooley addresses broader

16          aviation concerns, including compatibility with airstrips, helicopter operations, and drone

17          surveying, in her rebuttal testimony.




     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                  Page 7
  1               V.    REBUTTAL REGARDING HEALTH AND SAFETY CONCERNS

 2   Q.     THE DIRECT TESTIMONIES OF MULTIPLE INTERVENORS EXPRESS

 3          GENERAL CONCERNS ABOUT TRANSMISSION LINES PRODUCING EMF.

 4          WHAT VALUES DID APPLICANTS CALCULATE FOR THE PROJECT’S EMF,

 5          AND WHY ARE THOSE VALUES APPROPRIATE?

 6   A.     Applicants calculated the anticipated electric field values within and at the edge of the

 7          Project’s ROW (5.7 kV/meter and 4.0 kV/meter, respectively) and confirmed that they are

 8          well within the industry guidance described in IEEE Std C95.1-2019 – IEEE Standards for

 9          Safety Levels with Respect to Human Exposure to Electric, Magnetic, and Electromagnetic

10          Fields, 0 Hz to 300 GHz (10 kV/meter and 5 kV/meter, respectively), which was developed

11          and approved by a cross-functional group of industry experts with the express purpose to

12          “provide science-based exposure criteria to protect against established adverse health

13          effects in humans.”     Additionally, Applicants calculated the anticipated maximum

14          magnetic field value at the edge of the ROW to equal approximately 160 milligauss, which

15          is within their standard design criteria for 345 kV lines. These values are associated with

16          the peak loading the Proposed Transmission Line Project will experience. The measured

17          magnetic field at the edge of the ROW will be considerably less under typical operating

18          conditions. Taken together, by utilizing the structures described in response to question 5

19          of the Application, Applicants will design their system to limit EMF effects to values

20          typically seen on other lines across the state and in accordance with industry-recognized

21          standards. As Ms. Cooley explains in her rebuttal testimony, Applicants mitigate potential

22          EMF effects through appropriate ROW width design, increased phase-to-ground distance,

23          and compliance with the Commission’s policy of prudent avoidance.



     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                Page 8
  1   Q.     VARIOUS INTERVENORS SUBMITTED TESTIMONY VOICING GENERAL

 2          HEALTH AND SAFETY CONCERNS FOR PEOPLE AND ANIMALS LIVING

 3          NEAR OR UNDER THE PROPOSED TRANSMISSION LINE, SAFETY

 4          CONCERNS ABOUT LIGHTNING OCCURRING NEAR TRANSMISSION

 5          LINES AND OTHER POTENTIAL FIRE HAZARDS POSED BY TRANSMISSION

 6          LINES, INCLUDING ELECTRICAL ARCING RISKS. INTERVENOR THOMAS

 7          F. GREEN, P.E. (PAGE 40) EXPRESSES SPECIFIC CONCERNS WITH

 8          WILDFIRES CAUSED BY MOLTEN METALS EJECTED DURING “FAULT

9           INDUCED CONDUCTOR SLAP.” HOW DO APPLICANTS ADDRESS SAFETY

10          AND FIRE-RELATED CONCERNS SUCH AS THESE?

11   A.     Applicants’ standard practice is to install multiple grounding connections at each tower,

12          and they will maintain that practice for this Project. These grounding connections ensure

13          that there will be no risk of electrical shock to people or animals who come into contact

14          with the towers under nearly all conditions. Applicants will work with landowners to

15          ground metallic objects that will remain in the ROW after the Project is complete, such as

16          fences and gates. Provided that metallic parts of livestock enclosures, feeding and watering

17          troughs, and manmade beehives are properly grounded, there should be no adverse impacts

18          on animals within the Project’s ROW.

19                 Metallic floating (ungrounded) objects, such as tractors with rubber tires, can build

20          up charge when located within or immediately adjacent to the Project’s ROW, but safety

21          standards required by the National Electrical Safety Code (NESC) limit that amount of

22          charge to a sensation similar to touching a light switch after walking across the carpet in

23          wool socks.




     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                 Page 9
 1                  In regard to lightning, the same multiple grounding connections provide an

2           excellent path for energy from lightning strikes to travel safely to ground without adversely

3           impacting the surrounding area. Applicants have run lightning outage simulations on the

4           Proposed Transmission Line Project and found their proposed designs perform extremely

 5          well in resisting lightning-induced flashovers and outages.        These data point to an

 6          extremely low public safety risk.

 7                 Regarding wildfire risk, wildfires caused by transmission lines require an ignition

 8          source, either direct contact with the conductors to a flammable object (such as a dead tree)

 9          or material melting on the line and dripping onto a flammable object. Applicants mitigate

10          these risks through several means. First, Applicants selected an appropriate ROW width

11          (200 feet) to effectively execute their vegetation management program, which is designed

12          to prevent contact with the energized conductors and vegetation located both within and

13          outside the ROW. Second, Applicants are specifying components that meet or exceed

14          industry standards for mechanical strength and chemical properties that prevent the type of

15          damage required to drop a conductor from its normal position on the tower. Third,

16          Applicants’ selection of conductor for the Project limits the maximum temperature of the

17          energized components to well below their melting points, greatly reducing the potential for

18          an ignition source emanating from the Project’s facilities. Fourth, Applicants’ designs

19          include mechanical devices, called spacers, that prevent the conductors from “slapping”

20          together under wind and other circumstances, which also mitigates the possibility of molten

21          metal contacting an ignition source. Finally, if all those safeguards were to fail, the

22          Project’s facilities are designed with protection systems at each substation that de-energize

23          the line within 0.5 seconds or less in the event of a dropped wire situation. Taken together,




     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                 Page 10
  1          the risk for the Project to start a wildfire is extremely remote. Ms. Cooley’s rebuttal

 2          testimony provides additional detail on this topic, including on Applicants’ compliance

 3          with NESC, OSHA, ANSI, and IEEE standards.


 4   Q.     IN ADDITION TO FIRE RISKS, MULTIPLE INTERVENORS RAISED

 5          CONCERNS REGARDING POTENTIAL SAFETY RISKS THAT MAY BE

 6          ASSOCIATED WITH ELECTRIC FACILITIES IN GENERAL, SUCH AS

 7          CONDUCTOR FAILURE AND ICE LOADING.                            HOW DO APPLICANTS

 8          ADDRESS THESE POTENTIAL CONCERNS?

 9   A.     Electric transmission lines in the United States are subject to the requirements of the NESC,

10          which stipulate that structures must be able to withstand one-in-one-hundred-year extreme

11          wind events and one-in-fifty-year combined wind and ice events. The one-in-one-hundred-

12          year wind gust in the Project’s area is 95 miles per hour. Applicants’ design criteria exceed

13          the NESC’s requirements for combined wind and ice loading.


14   Q.     IN THE DIRECT TESTIMONY OF REX AND KELLI EMERSON (PAGE 1),

15          THEY EXPRESS THEIR CONCERN THAT A 500-FOOT SETBACK WILL

16          RENDER SIGNIFICANT PORTIONS OF THEIR PROPERTY UNUSABLE FOR

17          DEVELOPMENT. WHAT RESTRICTIONS DO APPLICANTS PLACE ON

18          LANDOWNERS OUTSIDE OF THE PROPOSED ROW?

19   A.     While Applicants established setbacks to certain facilities for route segment development,

20          they purposely selected their proposed 200-foot ROW such that there will be no restrictions

21          on future development outside of it. Applicants may require removal of “danger trees”

22          located outside of the ROW that pose a safety risk to the transmission line, but they will

23          not impose any restrictions on the use or enjoyment of any lands outside of the Project’s


     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                 Page 11
 1           proposed ROW and will design their facilities to maintain safe operating distances to

2           anything built outside of it.


3    Q.     THE DIRECT TESTIMONIES OF SEVERAL INTERVENORS EXPRESS

4           SAFETY CONCERNS WITH ACTIVE IMPLANTABLE MEDICAL DEVICES

 5          (AIMDS), SUCH AS INSULIN PUMPS AND PACEMAKERS, IN PROXIMITY TO

 6          HIGH-VOLTAGE POWER LINES.                   WHAT CAUTIONS SHOULD PEOPLE

 7          WITH SUCH DEVICES TAKE WHEN NAVIGATING UNDER OR NEAR THE

 8          765 KV LINES?

 9   A.     It is theoretically possible for the EMF from a power line to interfere with an AIMD.

10          However, Applicants are unaware of any instances of a person in the United States coming

11          to harm because of electrical interference with AIMDs. Applicants encourage anyone with

12          an AIMD to consult with their medical professional regarding the specific EMF-related

13          design characteristics of their implant.


14   Q.     THE DIRECT TESTIMONIES OF MULTIPLE INTERVENORS EXPRESSED

15          SAFETY CONCERNS WITH APPLICANTS’ PERSONNEL HAVING ACCESS

16          TO THE ROW DURING CONSTRUCTION AND MAINTENANCE ACTIVITIES.

17          SIMILARLY, THE DIRECT TESTIMONIES OF MULTIPLE INTERVENORS

18          EXPRESSED CONCERNS WITH DAMAGED FENCES AND OPEN GATES

19          PROVIDING ACCESS TO TRESPASSERS AND POACHERS.                                    PLEASE

20          ADDRESS THESE CONCERNS.

21   A.     During construction, Applicants maintain several layers of oversight of construction crews,

22          including a foreman, onsite field construction coordinators, and a Construction Manager

23          responsible for all aspects of the project. These individuals are responsible for ensuring


     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                               Page 12
  1          compliance with Applicants’ construction specifications, which include specific

 2          requirements for use of the ROW. Among other things, LCRA TSC’s construction

 3          specification requires that:

 4                 •   All gates that are closed and locked when encountered will be kept

 5                     closed and locked immediately after use.

 6                 •   The contractor’s activities are restricted to the ROW unless access

 7                     across private property has been coordinated with the landowner or

 8                     tenant.

 9                 •   No fences may be taken down without prior permission from the

10                     property owner or tenant, and any fences removed must be replaced to

11                     their original condition.

12          Additionally, Applicants will perform routine inspections utilizing internal resources.

13          Those resources are subject to routine background checks and are held to the same

14          requirements and similar levels of oversight as construction crews.


15   Q.     MULTIPLE INTERVENORS EXPRESS GENERAL CONCERNS REGARDING

16          IMPACTS TO LOCAL ROADS AND TRAFFIC DURING CONSTRUCTION

17          ACTIVITIES,          PARTICULARLY         THE     ABILITY       OF    LOCAL       FIRST

18          RESPONDERS TO NAVIGATE ROADS WHILE CONSTRUCTION IS IN-

19          PROGRESS. PLEASE DISCUSS HOW APPLICANTS WILL ADDRESS THESE

20          CONCERNS.

21   A.     Applicants intend to keep existing roads, access routes, and rights-of-way open and

22          passable throughout construction to the extent practical. There may be temporary traffic



     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                            Page 13
 1           delays or brief closures during activities such as wire stringing, material deliveries, or

2           heavy equipment movement. Applicants’ personnel will be onsite during those activities

3           to manage traffic control and minimize impacts to property access and the traveling public.

 4          Applicants will promptly adjust their construction activities when necessary to allow first

 5          responders to travel through the Project area.

 6                 Additionally, Applicants will identify anticipated heavy haul and construction

 7          access routes early in the project and coordinate with the appropriate local or county

 8          officials as necessary. If roadway improvements, reinforcement, or repairs are required as

 9          a direct result of project construction activities, Applicants will work with the applicable

10          entity to determine the appropriate scope, responsibility, and timing. Applicants are

11          committed to maintaining roads in a passable condition throughout construction and will

12          address project-related impacts as appropriate.


13   Q.     SEVERAL INTERVENORS EXPRESSED CONCERNS WITH APPLICANTS’

14          ABILITY TO SAFELY OPERATE AND MAINTAIN STRUCTURES IN AREAS

15          THAT EXPERIENCED SIGNIFICANT FLOODING IN JULY 2025. HOW DO

16          YOU RESPOND TO THOSE CONCERNS?

17   A.     I was onsite in Kerrville and Hunt on July 5, 2025, performing damage assessment

18          activities on behalf of LCRA TSC. The impacts of that flooding event were immense.

19          Following the event, I performed a comprehensive review of LCRA TSC’s criteria for

20          foundation designs within floodplains and floodways, which were last updated in the

21          summer of 2021. I determined that LCRA TSC’s current criteria significantly avoid the

22          impacts of severe flooding. This conclusion was validated by the actual performance of

23          LCRA TSC’s transmission structures in the areas that experienced the most extreme



     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                Page 14
  1          flooding. LCRA TSC’s tubular steel poles and lattice tower structures placed on circular

 2          concrete piers, which are similar to those proposed from this Project, experienced no

 3          discernable damage. Based on this analysis and experience, I am confident in the

 4          Applicants’ ability to design structures that can withstand major flooding events.


 5            VI.    REBUTTAL REGARDING COMPATIBILITY WITH COMMERCIAL
 6                                      OPERATIONS

 7   Q.     INTERVENOR JASON HOWTON (PAGE 21) EXPRESSES MULTIPLE

 8          CONCERNS WITH THE PROJECT IN PROXIMITY TO ACTIVE LIMESTONE

 9          QUARRIES, INCLUDING IMPACTS FROM ROCK BLASTING ACTIVITIES

10          AND DUST CONTAMINATION.                  HOW DO APPLICANTS ADDRESS SUCH

11          ACTIVITIES IN THE PROJECT AREA?

12   A.     Applicants’ reinforced concrete foundations and steel structural supports are designed to

13          withstand repeated cyclic loading from wind gusts without experiencing fatigue failure or

14          cracking. This subjects the structures to dynamic loading in a manner that is comparable

15          to the vibrations Mr. Howton describes in his direct testimony. Mr. Howton also expresses

16          concerns regarding hardware loosening due to these vibrations. Applicants install locking

17          devices (such as jam nuts, pin-lock nuts, and palnuts) on all bolted connections that are

18          specifically designed to withstand such vibrations and maintain snug connections.

19          Additionally, Mr. Howton expresses concerns about the effects of air pressure from

20          blasting activities on the overhead components of the Project, specifically the excitation of

21          conductor oscillation across multi-span sections of the line. Applicants are designing the

22          Project to withstand 95 mile-per-hour wind gusts. I am unaware of any blasting activities

23          occurring outside of the Project’s 200-foot-wide ROW that would generate wind pressures




     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                  Page 15
  1          on the Project’s facilities that would exceed those caused by 95 miles-per-hour wind gusts.

 2          Finally, Mr. Howton expresses concern with contamination buildup on the Project’s

 3          facilities as a result of nearby quarry activities. Applicants address this concern by

 4          installing high-voltage insulators with coatings that resist the accumulation of such

 5          contaminants in areas immediately adjacent to sources of contamination, such as quarries

 6          and power plants.


 7   Q.     THE DIRECT TESTIMONY OF JIM LUTHER, ON BEHALF OF THE BURNET

 8          COUNTY COMMISSIONERS COURT, EXPRESSED CONCERN THAT THE

 9          PROJECT MAY INTERFERE WITH 911 COMMUNICATIONS THAT ARE

10          TRANSMITTED           VIA    RADIO      TOWERS.           PLEASE       DESCRIBE        ANY

11          ANTICIPATED COMMUNICATIONS INTERFERENCE WITH DEVICES USED

12          ON PROPERTIES CROSSED BY A TRANSMISSION LINE SUCH AS THIS.

13   A.     Applicants have performed preliminary engineering studies and determined that the

14          anticipated radio interference associated with the Project is within the guidance specified

15          for signal degradation in IEEE Std 430-2017 – IEEE Standard Procedures for the

16          Measurement of Radio Noise from Overhead Power Lines and Substations. Additionally,

17          transmission lines, such as those the Applicants will install as part of the Project, operate

18          at extremely low frequencies (ELF). As such, the only known potential communication

19          interferences occur on similarly low-frequency bands, such as AM Radio. High-frequency

20          signals, such as cellular, global positioning systems (GPS), and microwave bands, operate

21          at frequencies that will not be impacted by the Project. As Ms. Cooley confirms in her

22          rebuttal testimony, Applicants operate their own communication systems in close




     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                 Page 16
  1          proximity to transmission lines without adverse impact, and the Project is unlikely to cause

 2          substantial interference with nearby electronic devices or communications equipment.


 3                       VII.     REBUTTAL REGARDING COST ESTIMATES

 4   Q.     DESCRIBE THE APPLICANTS’ APPROACH TO DEVELOPING COST

 5          ESTIMATES FOR THE PROJECT.

 6   A.     To prepare for this proceeding, Applicants spent months developing and refining their cost

 7          estimating approach. Prior to estimating routes included in this Application, each utility

 8          compared their respective cost models and their results together. Applicants ultimately

 9          found that when each utility appropriately applied its respective structure spotting

10          procedures and contingency percentages, their estimates aligned extremely well, despite

11          certain variations in their respective inputs. Based on that alignment, Applicants agreed to

12          proceed with a unified cost approach that utilized Oncor’s cost model in combination with

13          each respective utility’s spotting procedures and contingency percentages for their

14          respective portions of the line. This approach ensured consistency in structure spotting

15          across all links and, therefore, uniformity in estimating all links, which, in turn, created

16          accurate differentiation between routes to best inform the Commission in selecting the final

17          route. While Oncor developed the estimates in the Application, LCRA TSC reviewed the

18          final cost estimates and Oncor’s methodology for developing those estimates, which

19          confirmed that Oncor’s engineering staff correctly applied LCRA TSC’s spotting

20          requirements and the appropriate contingencies to LCRA TSC’s portion of the Project.

21          These actions led LCRA TSC to have a high level of confidence in the estimates and LCRA

22          TSC’s ability to execute the Project for its 50 percent portion of the costs.




     Elliott Rebuttal Testimony                                                                Page 17
  1   Q.     THE DIRECT TESTIMONY OF INTERVENOR FREDERICK B. WULFF JR., ON

 2          BEHALF OF WULFF BLUFF CREEK RANCH, LTD. AND ITS PARTNERS

 3          (PAGE 11), EXPRESSED CONCERNS REGARDING THE STRUCTURE

 4          COUNTS REFLECTED IN THE COST ESTIMATES. HOW DO YOU RESPOND?

 5   A.     Mr. Wulff’s concerns appear to be based on an incomplete understanding of Applicants’

 6          structure spotting procedures. He specifically cites Link N12, which, in his judgment,

 7          requires 12 dead end structures. He notes that the cost worksheet used to justify the

 8          estimates in the Application included 18 dead end structures for this segment and uses that

 9          difference to conclude that the cost estimates are essentially the “Applicants’ ranking of

10          their engineers’ preference on which route to build.” That characterization is incorrect. In

11          developing his count of 12 dead end structures, Mr. Wulff overlooks the fact that there are

12          three power line crossings in Link N12, which per LCRA TSC’s spotting procedures

13          require dead end structures on both sides. Additionally, Link N12 crosses a four-lane

14          divided highway, which also requires dead end structures on both sides per LCRA TSC’s

15          spotting procedures. Finally, the forward progressing routes on both ends of Link N12

16          require line angles large enough to necessitate the use of a dead end structure. Altogether,

17          these requirements, the number of structures with angles greater than fifteen degrees and
